\[
L(\cdot;\, t) = g(\cdot;\, t) * I,
\quad
N(\cdot;\, t) = \begin{cases}
  t^{\gamma/2}\, |\nabla L| & \text{gradient} \\
  t^{\gamma}\, (L_{xx} + L_{yy}) & \text{Laplacian} \\
  t^{2\gamma}\, (L_{xx} L_{yy} - L_{xy}^2) & \text{Hessian}
\end{cases}
\qquad
t_i = \sigma_i^2,
\quad
\sigma_i = \sigma_0 \left(\frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_0}\right)^{i/(n-1)},
\quad
I_{\text{out}} = N(\cdot;\, t_{i^*}),
\quad
i^* = \arg\max_i |N(\cdot;\, t_i)|,
\qquad
\sigma_0 = 1,\ \sigma_{\max} = 4,\ n = 5,\ \gamma = 1
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(I\): The input channel
- \(L\): The scale space, the image blurred by a Gaussian of variance t
- \(t, \sigma\): The scale t = sigma^2, in pixels squared
- \(L_x, L_{xx}, L_{xy}\): Derivatives of L along x and y. y points down.
- \(N\): The normalized measure
- \(\gamma\): The normalization power
- \(n\): The number of scales in the stack

L is the image blurred by a Gaussian g of variance t, the scale space of the image. Its derivatives come from derivative-of-Gaussian kernels cut at 4 sigma, as in scipy.ndimage.gaussian_filter. Derivatives get weaker as t grows, so plain responses at different scales cannot be compared. Lindeberg multiplies a derivative of order m by t^(m gamma / 2). With gamma 1, a structure made s times larger gives the same normalized responses at scale s^2 t as the original gives at t. So the scale where the normalized response is strongest grows with the size of the structure. Lindeberg detects features as local maxima over space and scale. This filter takes, at each pixel, the largest absolute value over the stack, so it gives a value at every pixel. Ties go to the smaller sigma. The scale output is the sigma of that scale.
